This research paper delves into the anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction model, where a two-level system interacts with a quantized electromagnetic field in the presence of relaxation and pure dephasing. Despite damping, the system is capable of producing maximally entangled anti-Jaynes-Cummings states and executing Rabi oscillations, as evidenced by the entanglement and antipolarization degree of the outcoming photons. Furthermore, the study offers a method for estimating the average entanglement level of these states as a function of the system's energy relaxation and pure dephasing rates.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warning signs for cardiovascular diseases. To improve this process, our system automates the analysis of ECG signals to calculate heart rate variability (HRV) characteristics, such as standard deviation of NN intervals, mean NN interval duration, and NN interval difference variability. We've also optimized the algorithm to reduce computational time, which is currently less than 6 milliseconds per sample.

We analyze large deviations of power input by an active force on an Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle (AOUP) within or outside a confining barrier. This involves calculating the rate function for the particle's average energy within a steady-state equilibrium. Employing a fluctuation relation, this rate function can be obtained from the frequency of rare, extreme events in the particle's position and velocity. These calculations are performed for both free and confined scenarios in harmonic potentials, utilizing a semi-analytical approach that involves solving a set of nonlinear equations. The results reveal a frequent occurrence of high energy states in the free scenario, which significantly drops when the system is confined. Moreover, the rate function for the confined scenario closely resembles that of a passive overdamped harmonic oscillator.

This research introduces the HUMBI dataset, a comprehensive collection of multiview
human body images, captured through high-definition video and stills, as well as
inertial sensor data, to record a person's movements in three-dimensional space.
The HUMBI dataset features five individuals, dressed in eight different outfits,
viewed from five angles while they perform various movements, which are further
documented through inertial sensor recordings. To accurately replicate the
inertial sensor data, a simulation model was also developed. The dataset will be
utilized to improve the creation of more realistic virtual human characters by
enhancing the fit of clothing simulations and refining inertial navigation systems.

Despite the growing need for models in non-English languages, natural language processing has long been Anglo-centric, and translating neural models between languages can be costly and time-consuming. We propose a universal framework that allows us to transfer neural models from English to over 100 other languages with minimal overhead, and as a result, enables the rapid creation of high-performance models for languages that previously had limited models. Our approach and the resulting models will be made freely available.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being a highly performing and efficient benchmark. Building upon this framework, we introduce refinements that enhance its accuracy. Firstly, we incorporate a more comprehensive propagation method using a higher-order grid, aiming to capture spatial relationships in recurrent VSR. Secondly, we design a module to utilize optical flow in aligning feature maps extracted from different frames within a recursive RFSR framework. With these modifications, the proposed method demonstrates improved performance with a reduced number of recursive iterations, achieving superior results across multiple benchmark datasets while being relatively more computationally efficient.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we present a simple
yet effective solution where each task has its own dedicated dynamics model.

There is no single universal protocol that achieves maximum efficiency in finite-time stochastic heat engines for all possible temperatures and scaling conditions. Even when temperature and a key scaling parameter are fixed and within a certain range, the optimal protocol depends on a third scaling parameter, which is inherent in the system. A practical solution involves developing a simple, general, and nearly optimal protocol that works well across a wide range of temperatures and scaling conditions without requiring any initial knowledge of the system.

This research proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing the impact of combined hurricane and storm surge events on large power grids. To simulate real-world hurricane scenarios, the study generates probabilistic storm paths based on historical data, and corresponding storm surge situations are developed based on actual hurricane parameters. To assess potential losses, the study employs a quantitative metric that estimates total load reduction, and these outcomes are calculated through simulation-based averaging. The proposed method is demonstrated using a 1200-bus network set within a geographic area affected by a real-world hurricane, and the associated storm surge, to analyze its impact.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

We've developed a family of generalized heterochaos baker maps that combine a classic chaotically behaved y-map with its inverse, x-map, inverted and mirrored, to create a new, hybrid area-preserving system. These novel maps exhibit unique characteristics, such as expansive behavior on an atomic scale, effectively creating a type of 'atomic chaos.' Through our research, we identified the essential conditions necessary for the creation of chaotic systems using the y-map and the converse for the x-map, and found that the resulting hybrid maps inevitably produce chaotic outcomes, regardless of the y-map's dynamics. Furthermore, by analyzing the first digit frequencies of both the naturally occurring and inversely derived iterates of these hybrid maps, we discovered that they conform to either Benford's law or its inverse counterpart, depending on the nature of the y-map, and found corresponding frequency distributions for other digit positions, conditioned on the initial starting point's decimal expansion.

Following the groundbreaking detection of the Higgs boson in 2012, the field of particle physics has entered an exciting period. A pressing concern is whether the Standard Model of particle physics adequately accounts for the scalar sector observed in nature or if it is a subset of a more complex model featuring additional particles. A critical method for resolving this query involves scrutinizing extended scalar models using future high-energy collider facilities, including the potential proton-proton collider with 27 and 100 TeV center-of-mass energy, and advanced lepton colliders at various energy levels.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic Network (QPNet) capable of generating audio waveforms with precise control over the pitch and duration. By combining a pitch-dependent dilated convolutional layer with transposed 1D convolution, QPNet effectively produces a waveform from a weighted kernel that remains invariant across different frames at a given pitch. This invariance, paired with adaptive kernel truncation based on the duration, enables the model to generate outputs of various temporal lengths from a fixed, pitch-dependent kernel size. Furthermore, the model leverages a quasi-periodic weighting system to prioritize spectral correlations within each pitch bin, resulting in a more accurate synthesis.

Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF), the dominant method, have widespread use today. Despite CF's efficiency for several years, its limitations are now more pronounced due to the emergence of more sophisticated techniques. This paper overviews the advancements in CF's improvements over the past two decades, focusing on innovative approaches to address its earlier shortcomings. These developments address four key problems: (1) scalability and data sparsity; (2) large datasets and complex user behavior; (3) heterogeneous and multi-modal data; and (4) explainability and transparency in recommendations.

Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators that better reflect a star's magnetic behavior is essential for distinguishing these signals from a planet's Doppler signal. In this study, we employed a machine-learning approach to find these indicators among the vast spectral dataset provided by the DELS project, which observed a sample of active stars with high spectral resolution. By using a deep learning model, we analyzed the spectral datasets and identified two new indicators at 430nm that outperform the traditional S index in terms of correlation with magnetic activity levels. These indicators also demonstrated better performance in detecting short-term activity fluctuations and better scaled to longer-term activity patterns, according to spectral observations taken over several nights.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, a new approach is taken. The average tunneling rate is measured over a specific temperature range, not the conductance as measured at a single temperature. The impact of this method on detecting Majorana modes in InAs/Al bilayers is explored. The results show that a broad distribution of zero-energy peaks can be distinguished from a single Majorana peak by measuring the area under the conductance curve rather than its peak height at a single temperature. This distinction can be achieved by operating in a relatively warm temperature range (approximately 300 mK to 1.2 K) without needing sophisticated signal processing techniques.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence.

When attempting image enhancement or editing tasks, there may not be a single, definitive outcome. To address this, we have developed a approach that incorporates user-supplied patches along with guidance from relevant labels, which can be applied to various tasks such as inpainting, detail enhancement, or restoration. Our method is implemented as a global optimization problem and is solved using a structured message passing algorithm derived from the influence function, resulting in a computationally efficient solution. Our experiments demonstrate that it outperforms existing techniques by a significant margin, particularly in situations where the provided patches overlap with critical areas of the image.

This technical report showcases the winning model of the QuoVista challenge, a machine learning competition focused on long-form video understanding. The challenge involved predicting human edited points in video content from unannotated source videos. We detail a two-stage approach our team employed, incorporating both feature extraction and matching modules, and highlight key decision-making considerations throughout the design process. Additionally, we discuss the difficulties encountered in training and model optimization due to the scarcity and irregular distribution of video data.

This study's findings provide initial insight into snow deposition dynamics by
combining laboratory measurements with numerical simulations. In the laboratory,
snow particles were observed in a turbulent airflow with varying flux and correlation
properties similar to observed snow crystal movements. The goal was to identify the
critical factors influencing snow particle clustering and accumulation in the study.
When exposed to the same airflow, different snow crystal types displayed distinct
cluster patterns and settling behaviors, which were linked to their unique shapes and
orientations. The numerical simulations confirmed that the particles' translational and
rotational movements, as well as their orientations, contribute significantly to their
settling patterns. The simulations revealed that the particles' rotational motion is fully
determined by their initial conditions, even though their translational motion is partly
independent. The particles' sticking together during clustering does not affect their
overall distribution, which is controlled by their initial conditions.

A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, which is then updated through a continuous interplay with the environment. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application has been mainly confined to straightforward scenarios. This study seeks to expand the boundaries of active inference by tackling a more complex challenge: simultaneous metric and topological navigation within a dynamic environment. To achieve this, we introduce a novel and efficient algorithm that incorporates various constraints directly into the mental framework's formation. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through multiple simulations featuring increasingly complex scenarios.

In experimental facilities specializing in high energy physics, nuclear physics, and cosmology, the task of processing large amounts of data in real-time is a significant challenge. The capacity of memory and processing power must be predicted with high accuracy to avoid data loss and ensure sufficient storage. A statistical method called the modified filter method (FM) has been developed to forecast both the number of events accepted into online analysis and the total event count, including those lost due to memory constraints. FM has been successfully applied and validated in operations with multiple event data sets from the Dark Energy Survey and the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope.

Utilizing Finzi's gravity theory that enhances interactions at large scales, we analyze galaxy clusters from a thermodynamic perspective, establishing a statistical model to derive thermodynamic equations and comparing clustering behavior with Newtonian gravity. We also explore the general distribution function's behavior as the clustering parameter varies in strength, with the finding that phase transitions are feasible, albeit hierarchically organized.

A type of convex geometric hypergraph, known as cgh, comprises a set of subsets originating from strictly convex point sets in the plane. In this study, researchers explore a specific type of problem associated with cghs: saturation problems that correspond to earlier studied extremal issues. Using a mathematical approach, the study determines the maximum capacity of certain geometrically separated groups of points and establishes an exact value for a specific instance, as well as approximate values for seven out of eight possible geometric hypergraph configurations up to a specific level of accuracy, and a related but less accurate figure for the eighth configuration.

To gain a better understanding of the relative contributions of different processes, the angular distributions and energy spectra of $\alpha$ and deuterons resulting from breakup, transfer, and incomplete fusion have been measured and calculated. Cross-sections for the $^6$Li + $^{12}$C system were experimentally measured at energies near the Coulomb barrier, with calculations via coupled reaction calculations confirming the experimental results. These studies provide a comprehensive analysis of the reaction mechanisms involved.

A previously overlooked ability in bio-inspired snake robots is dynamic vertical climbing. A novel locomotion technique mimicking the Pacific Lamprey's movement has been discovered, which enables a robot to navigate on flat surfaces while climbing at near-vertical inclines. A simplified model has been created to illustrate the robot's ability to ascend by generating upward motion, and subsequent experimental trials were conducted to refine this movement. The resulting robot, Trident, was able to successfully navigate at inclines of up to 84 degrees and achieve a peak vertical travel distance of 3.3 times its length. Furthermore, experiments revealed that increasing the frequency and amplitude of the lateral movement predictably enhances vertical progression. This innovative method of vertical climbing using horizontal motion has significant potential in robotic applications where height differences need to be overcome.

This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework designed to identify the most effective combinations of treatments in cases of colon cancer-induced immune response. An Itō stochastic process models the colon cancer dynamics, whose probabilistic evolution is governed by the Fokker-Planck equation. To identify optimal treatment combinations, an open-loop control optimization issue is proposed. Simulation results demonstrating the use of Doxorubicin chemotherapy and IL-2 immunotherapy validate the introduced framework.

This study presents an innovative approach to managing D2D communications by optimizing real-time data exchange through a dynamic scheduling technique focused on response time and throughput. Our proposed method incorporates the Parallel Task Scheduling algorithm to reduce the overhead of D2D channel allocation. A two-stage process is employed, including stage one that uses the Parallel Task Scheduling algorithm to generate a channel allocation sequence and stage two where we apply the Modified Shortest Job First to schedule the tasks based on their arrival times and processing requirements. Our goal is to minimize the response time and maximize the system's throughput while ensuring system stability. We achieved this by adjusting the system's arrival rate and showed that our method can be adjusted to maintain optimal results. Our approach was validated through simulations that compared its performance to other established scheduling methods like First Come First Serve and Shortest Job First.

Moffatt first discussed the concept of helicity in a fluid without viscosity in reference [25] and explored its preservation in the case of barotropic, compressible flow with smooth solutions. This paper demonstrates that weak solutions to this system in a specific mathematical space ensure the conservation of helicity. Additionally, similar results were found for both homogeneous incompressible Euler equations and the surface quasi-geostrophic equation.

The researchers in a particular study extended the solutions found in \cite{Hsiou2018} to find more general solutions for the 2D Helmholtz equation in the context of complex geometric optics and scattering theory. By applying a result from \cite{Morris2013} that involved a conformal transformation, they were able to obtain expressions for the solutions expressed as a sum of geometric optics expressions for an arbitrary number of point sources located within a domain. After conducting some analytical calculations based on the expression for one source, they found that the coherent superposition of the logarithmic phase term and the harmonic function could represent the geodesic ray equation. Furthermore, by analyzing the far-field scattering data, they were able to derive an expression for the scattering amplitude in terms of the location of point sources and the far-field scattering data, which was confirmed through numerical validation.

Calculations involving the orbital dynamics of merging compact binary systems,
including higher-order effects of gravitational wave radiation, reveal that late-time
eccentricities of inspiraling binaries are typically underestimated by standard
models by up to 30 percent for heavy systems like 300-solar-mass binaries at
10 Hz, and less so for lighter binaries. By incorporating more refined equations,
a novel, accurate analytic formula for eccentricities at late times is formulated.
Furthermore, this model's results remain largely insensitive to the masses of the
binary components, with deviations below two percent, and generalizes previous
work by Peters and Mathews.

A proposed innovation, the X-ray free-electron laser (X-FEL), has the potential to greatly increase the efficiency of free-electron lasers (FELs) by utilizing electron beam modulation. This can be achieved through interaction with a transverse optical laser field at the entrance of an undulator, which creates notable effects on electron beam trajectory and radiation field at specific phases due to the electron beam's short lifetime and small scale. This results in a highly intense coherent X-ray source with a unique ability to produce extremely short pulses, specifically in the few femtosecond range. This source could significantly impact various fields such as protein research, crystallography, and high-energy physics.

Event identification is crucial in graph data analysis, yet detecting occurrences in evolving networks poses difficulties due to a limited number of data points available for each event and varying duration of subgraphs within the main network. To overcome these challenges, we've created an approach that combines a novel, dynamic graph representation with a temporal self-transferring learning method for event recognition. First, a new representation for evolving networks is developed using a novel set of temporal graph structures paired with a temporal autoencoder to extract meaningful features from subgraphs and the main graph. Subgraph representations are then obtained through a temporal graph structure decomposition. Secondly, we leverage these feature extracts as the building blocks for training event recognition models, employing both static and dynamic features to inform our method. Finally, we present comprehensive experimental evaluations that showcase our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods for event recognition.

The solutions of the Guderley problem involving an imploding shock wave in an ideal gas are examined, focusing on how a power law initial density distribution affects the accelerating shock. This is achieved through in-depth analysis of self-similar solutions and their similarity exponents under different symmetry conditions and varying parameters of adiabatic index and spatial density exponent. Moreover, we show how these theoretical solutions can be accurately matched to numerical simulations, thereby determining the similarity exponents and asymptotic behavior of precisely defined radial density distributions. Ultimately, our work provides a thorough explanation of how varying density distributions affect shock behavior and offers a means to accurately determine similarity exponents through comparison with numerical simulations.

The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has created a pressing need for their explanations. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by decomposing these systems into more understandable components through explanation. In this context, we introduce a novel approach that furnishes explanations for black-box deep learning models by harnessing the predictive power of interpretable models formed from visual and textual components. By training these components on image and text features extracted from scenario descriptions and problem statements, we establish a framework that can provide clear explanations for their predictions in specific contexts. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated in two real-world use cases involving automated document scanning.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to tailor endoscopic surveillance and treatment, thereby preventing unnecessary procedures.  This process typically involves examining hematoxylin-eosin stained tissue sections, which are time-consuming and require significant pathologist expertise for accurate diagnosis.  Our work addresses these challenges by developing a deep learning-based method for identifying polyp types from histopathology images, even when stained surface regions are not provided.  By analyzing whole-slide images of 540 cases with 1940 images, our model demonstrated a 0.83 AUC across eight classes and 0.87 AUC for high-risk neoplastic polyp detection.  Notably, our model achieved these results without relying on stained surface images, which are often difficult to obtain in certain clinical settings.

In the context of zero-error source coding, our investigation focuses on how much information a guesser can reveal about the source, where the guesser has access to a noisy version of the encoded message. The source coding problem with an adversarial guesser involves determining the minimum encoded message length that achieves a specific level of source knowledge for the guesser. The problem we're examining involves restricting the guesser's possibilities to a set of probabilities less than or equal to epsilon. The scenario we're looking at involves a source with n symbols, where the guesser has access to a noisy encoded message that involves a noisy channel with a stochastic matrix. The noise matrix and the source distribution are known. The optimal performance of this problem is measured in terms of the maximum amount of information that can be revealed to the guesser, where the source knows everything and the guesser has access to a perfect version of the encoded message. When the source knows everything and the guesser has access to a perfect version of the encoded message, this problem is equivalent to finding the maximum amount of information that can be revealed to the guesser in a source coding problem with an adversarial guesser. The optimal performance of this problem was previously known when the source distribution is uniform and there is no noise in the channel. Our work involves generalizing the optimal performance of this problem when the source distribution is not uniform and there is noise in the channel.

Deep learning-trained generative models can function as a prior in various inverse problems, such as generating high-quality images from limited, processed data. A key constraint in this process is determining how to accurately represent and utilize the generative model, particularly when working with vast datasets. A recently proposed method involves treating the generative model as a distribution and recovering it through maximum likelihood estimation using an array of noising transformations and numerous iterations. Our research demonstrates that this process not only fails to converge to the original distribution but also leads to unstable results when employed in generative modeling. To overcome these challenges, we present a new and efficient algorithm that allows accurate representation and utilization of the generative model, and showcases its effectiveness in tasks like image reconstruction, deconvolution, and compressive sensing through the application of multiple noising transformations and the utilization of a single, stable prior distribution.

A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant employs a combined quantum-classical strategy to achieve approximate solutions for complex optimization issues.  To optimize the QAOA's performance, we modified it by varying the angles within the qubit circuit and evaluated the impact of different measures, such as solution quality and approximate tolerance achievement rate. Utilizing the IBMQ noiseless simulator and IBMQ 20-qubit Essex processor, we tested our modified QAOA on the exact covering, vehicle routing, and MaxCut problems. The results indicate that the method of evaluating angles based on solution quality produces the best outcomes, with a higher success rate of achieving the approximate tolerance compared to a conventional angle choice that prioritizes circuit depth.

A comprehensive approach is presented for determining the segment area between an ellipse and a secant line, which is deflected when in the standard ellipse equation, either the major or minor axis serves as the secant line. The deflection gives rise to two distinct cases where one tangent line is involved, and the secant line intersects at two points. The proposed method successfully resolves these scenarios and provides a valid solution for all possible secant line positions, except those acting as tangent lines. Furthermore, the derived area formula incorporates both standard and generalized ellipse forms.

Building upon the work by Wang et al. (2020) for reinforcement learning, we examine the continuous-time counterpart of Q-learning under the entropy-regularized exploratory process framework. The paper establishes that the q-function is closely related to the instantaneous advantage rate function. The relationship holds specifically for the advantage reward function in the context of continuous-time Q-learning for any given state. Additionally, we develop a soft actor-critic algorithm based on this relationship and demonstrate its policy and value function convergence. The convergence of the estimated q-function to its true counterpart is also established. A key advantage of this new algorithm is its lack of requirement for model Inverse Reward Weighting (IRW) and the need to scale rewards by the average advantage rate is eliminated. The algorithm is analogous to SARSA, making it a suitable candidate for practical applications due to its ease of implementation and computational efficiency.

Quantum magnets with low-dimensional systems are notable for their atypical magnetic field behavior, which often exhibits unusual phase transitions and intricate patterns. A specific type of triangular lattice Hubbard model has been explored through exact diagonalization of small clusters, revealing an unexpected magnetic excitation mode that vanishes at a critical point and reappears at another point without passing through it in between, a phenomenon previously observed in low-dimensional quantum magnets. This vanishing and re-emergence of the mode is linked to two zero modes that arise due to symmetry and magnetic monopole properties and result in the breaking and reformation of a protection mechanism that inhibits certain magnetic excitations, a phenomenon previously observed in low-dimensional quantum magnets.

Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various clinical applications related to spine disorders. However, conventional methods can be hindered by several factors such as vertebral deformity, tumor, trauma, or aging-related spinal changes that affect radiograph image quality. This work aims to develop an advanced method for automatic vertebrae localization and identification in X-ray images with limited anatomical markers. Initially, a customized search region is established for each vertebra based on the position and size of the previous one. Next, a spine-dwelling convolutional neural network is employed to process the adjusted images within these regions, which are then used to generate and align vertebral candidates. Subsequently, a modified optimization algorithm is applied to refine the vertebral locations, followed by verification of the results to eliminate any false positives. Finally, a linked optimization process is used to adjust and optimize the vertebral locations accurately and efficiently. Compared to other state-of-the-art techniques, our approach demonstrated superior performance in terms of accuracy, sensitivity, and computational speed. Specifically, our method achieved mean dice similarity coefficients of 0.942 and 0.934 for L1-L5 vertebrae identification, respectively, with an average processing speed of 0.16 seconds per image.

Stochastic thermodynamics leverages Markovian jump processes to simulate spontaneous changes between quantifiable microscopic states. The flow rates of physical processes are calculated from the anti-symmetric transition measures defined on the network of states. The statistical fluctuations of these flow rates are analyzed by examining the moment-generating functions of the underlying jump processes. Specifically, we investigate the impact of two distinct ways to define these functions: one that prioritizes conservation laws and remains invariant under gauge transformations, and another that doesn't respect these constraints. We compare the accuracy of two methods for calculating fluctuation theorems using these moment-generating functions: one method relies on exact scaling and involves averaging over long periods of time, while the other involves asymptotic averaging over long periods of time. We find that although both methods yield similar results, the differences between them are only apparent when the averaging periods are shorter.

This research investigates how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it explores the change in relative quantum cohomology for toric complete intersections under two types of transformations: those preserving a divisor and those related to mirror symmetry. For the first type, it shows that the change in relative quantum cohomology is well-defined and can be expressed in terms of the original quantum cohomology. For the second type, it provides evidence that the change in relative quantum cohomology mirrors the change in its mirrored equivalent.

Two piezoelectric materials placed near each other can transfer energy across an intervening vacuum gap by transmitting acoustic waves. Our research provides a mathematical explanation for how this energy transfer occurs, and reveals that specific conditions allow for complete transmission of these waves. This finding holds true for materials of any shape or orientation and can be determined experimentally through measurement of surface properties. Furthermore, we analyzed the optimal energy transfer between identical zinc oxide crystals for various orientations and found a significant number of conditions that facilitate this energy transfer.

We examine a polariton condensate system consisting of two coupled microcavity systems, where one has a polariton reservoir excited by a diverse non-resonant profile, and the other has a polariton reservoir excited by a narrow linearly-polarized beam. The analysis shows that the narrow beam can be transformed into a broader, linearly-polarized output, and this new light can be directed at a tunable wavelength by adjusting the system's excitation parameters. This research also demonstrates a method to generate shorter-wavelength photons using this hybrid microcavity platform.

The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22b displays a unique pattern of temporal and spectral variations in its transit depths and is of significant interest due to its distinct characteristics. Several theories have been proposed to explain its origin, including the erosion of a planet by high-energy radiation, a debris disk that is not necessarily associated with a planet, and two alternative scenarios of atmospheric gas and of shattered rocks falling into the host star. To gain a better comprehension of the displanetary environment, we have conducted a thorough investigation of the displanetary environment by cross-analysing the observational data from the Hubble Space Telescope and the Spitzer Space Telescope, employing the dust modelling and spectral fitting techniques. Our findings indicate that the best-fitting model is a static disk model with two distinct dust populations, comprising fine and coarse particles, and a and a decreasing trend in the scale height as we move towards the star. Our analysis also reveals that the disk is being heated by two mechanisms, and the fine particles are being heated by starlight, while the coarse particles are being heated by the host star's gravitational energy. Our modelling indicates that the disk is rich in small particles and large boulders, and the amount of mass in these particles is sufficient to explain the observed variations in transit depths. Our findings also suggest that the disk is evolving, and the amount of mass in small particles is decreasing over time, and the amount of mass in large boulders is increasing. We develop a novel algebro-geometric approach to studying the Milnor fibration and establish a significant condition for holomorphic function deformations to maintain the Milnor fibration intact. In consequence, we derive a strategy to divide the space of polynomials with a specified degree into discrete, localized segments where the diffeomorphism of the Milnor fibration remains unchanged within each category.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library for data analysis and linear algebra, inspired by R and Python, with over 20 million downloads. This study involves a comprehensive performance evaluation of Daany, focusing on its core functionalities: data manipulation, data analysis, and linear algebra operations. The evaluation, carried out on various platforms, uses a combination of benchmarking tools and realistic use case simulations to assess the system's performance.

Despite his reputation as a great scientist, there remains controversy over whether Galileo was more skilled in mathematics or physics. I argue that his expertise lay in mathematics, and this mathematical dominance naturally led him to emphasize experimentation and a methodical approach to science. In this paper, I examine the underlying reasons for the debate about Galileo's skills, and how his own accounts have been misleading. I then analyze his educational background, the social environment of Tuscany, and key episodes in his career that support my assertion that his mathematical talents took precedence over his physical ones.

The increasing recognition of Pre-main Sequence stars (PMS) as a vital factor in high-energy astrophysics necessitates a thorough examination of the processes of star and planet formation. Generalized thermodynamic properties, specifically the concept of temperature as a function of energy density, are essential in understanding deuterium freeze-out in star formation and will likely hold significance in other low-energy astrophysical events such as the formation of cometary cometary volatile-rich comets. We have adapted this approach to the chemical composition of stars and planets, with a focus on the basic elements carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and helium. By applying the principle of chemical equilibrium under non-thermal conditions in low-energy astrophysical events, we have derived expressions for the reaction rates of atomic and molecular collisions. These formulas account for the anomalous behavior of these elements within the framework of generalized thermodynamics and are valid across a broad range of energy densities. We have utilized these formulas to derive expressions for the H II region and the core collapse of stars, with a focus on the isothermal profile of these systems. We have also utilized these formulas to investigate the processes of deuterium and 3He nanodevice production, particularly the role of these elements in the formation of planets.

A comprehensive review of magnetic reconnection is provided, focusing on its application to both collisional and collisionless scenarios. The review begins with a brief introduction to the reconnection process and then delves into more intricate aspects, such as the role of electron interaction in 3D reconnections and the formation of current sheets. Through a combination of observational data, simulation outcomes, and theoretical analysis, the complex dynamics of reconnection are illuminated, particularly in the collisionless case. Key considerations in the review include the electron fluid's impact, the application of MHD as a first-order model, and the formation of singular structures, such as the electron current layer. The review aims to offer a thorough understanding of magnetic reconnection, encompassing both fundamental and advanced topics in the field.

This document provides a overview of the IRIS system, which is a type of advanced digital assistant that learns to understand problems and their solutions by interacting with a specialist. IRIS was designed to analyze the decision-making processes of its expert partner and develop effective problem-solving strategies through repeated collaboration. As a result, IRIS is capable of not only providing solution-based responses but also explaining its reasoning and justifying its answers with reference to previous conversations. Additionally, IRIS can provide natural-sounding summaries of its interaction with the expert, highlighting its query history, key achievements, and areas of improvement. IRIS's abilities will be demonstrated by way of example in problem-solving tasks within the domain of molecular design.
